content: Chest physiotherapy, commonly abbreviated as CPT, refers to a range of therapeutic interventions typically performed by respiratory therapists. These treatments aim to enhance breathing by facilitating the indirect removal of mucus from the airways of a patient. In Australia, this practice is also referred to as respiratory or cardiothoracic physiotherapy. One of the techniques employed in chest physiotherapy is clapping or percussion. This involves the therapist gently clapping on the patient’s chest, back, and the areas beneath the arms. While percussion has been shown to be effective in managing respiratory conditions in infants and children, its use in adults has significantly declined in Australia. This shift is largely due to the development of more effective, self-management-oriented treatment modalities. Modern alternatives to traditional percussion include the use of devices such as flutter or oscillating positive pressure devices, PEP (positive expiratory pressure) masks or devices, and structured exercise regimens. These approaches are designed to improve mucus clearance and enhance respiratory function. The prescribed exercises may include specific respiratory techniques, such as autogenic drainage, as well as general cardiovascular exercises. These activities not only assist in the removal of sputum but also improve the efficiency of oxygen uptake in the muscles, thereby supporting overall respiratory health. In Australia, the term physiotherapy is often reserved for treatments that are administered exclusively by a registered physiotherapist.
